capabilities.target: Supabase Postgres database via service role (bypasses row level security)
support_messages table (insert; row is rendered back to the customer)

inputs.source: Developer's direct prompt in the IDE
Customer-written ticket message submitted through the public support widget

instructions.note: No stated restriction confines queries to ticket-related tables implied by the developer's request; the service-role credential can reach any table, including integration_tokens.

elements.name: Supabase Postgres database (service role, row level security bypassed)

controls.name: IDE per-tool-call approval prompt showing raw SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model and shows the raw SQL text (approval_review_mode: raw_action), so it does not decay purely from model capability. Its real-world effectiveness still decays with approval volume (approval fatigue, SAFE-T1403): developers approving many calls per session are unlikely to scrutinize data values embedded in an otherwise normal-looking INSERT statement, and a multi-step chain where each call looks individually legitimate can still assemble into an exfiltration path.

controls.name: Pin and hash-verify the MCP server package version
controls.decay_rationale: Version pinning and hash verification do not depend on model capability; they prevent silently receiving a compromised update.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting database role scoped away from secrets tables
controls.decay_rationale: A credential that cannot read integration_tokens or other customers' rows severs that part of the path regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Outbound secret-pattern filter on writes to customer-visible tables
controls.decay_rationale: A pattern-based scanner for secret-like strings before insertion into customer-visible tables catches many but not all exfiltration attempts; encoding or splitting the secret could bypass it.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): customer ticket message injects instructions causing service-role read of integration tokens and exfiltration via customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: Customer submits a ticket message via the public support widget; the message contains prompt-injection instructions.

A routine developer request ('show me the latest open support tickets') causes the agent to read ticket rows, including the attacker-controlled message, over a service-role connection that bypasses row level security.
The injected instruction directs the agent to also query the integration_tokens table, reachable because the service role bypasses RLS and is not scoped away from it.
The agent inserts a reply into support_messages containing the harvested tokens; this table is rendered back to the customer who authored the original ticket.

findings.residual_rationale: The mechanical credit for the per-call raw_action approval gate would produce a floor of moderate (critical minus two tiers), but this scenario matches a known public incident pattern in which exactly this kind of gate failed: the chain is built from several individually plausible tool calls (read tickets, read a token table, insert a reply) that a developer approving many calls per session is unlikely to recognize as an attack in progress, and secret values are unlikely to be scrutinized inside an otherwise normal-looking SQL statement (SAFE-T1403 consent fatigue). Residual is rated high rather than the mechanical floor.

forecast.watch_signal: IDE adds an 'always allow' or session-wide auto-approve mode; median tool-call approvals per developer session rises; model upgraded to a version that produces more routine-looking multi-step SQL chains.

evidence.observation: The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database.
Rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, making that table an egress point out of the trust boundary.
Developers approve many calls in a session, indicating high approval volume consistent with approval fatigue.

recommendations.action: Replace the service role connection with a least-privilege, RLS-respecting role scoped to the tables the support agent needs, excluding integration_tokens and other secrets tables.
Add an outbound secret-pattern scanner on any write to a customer-visible table before it is committed.
Pin the MCP server package to a specific audited version and verify its hash instead of installing @latest.
Log and alert whenever a query sequence touches a secrets table (integration_tokens) within the same session as a customer-facing write.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server install (@latest) enables supply chain tampering (ASI04, SAFE-T1201)

attack_path.note: Attacker publishes a compromised or backdoored version of @supabase/mcp-server-supabase.
npx -y always fetches the latest published version with no pinning or hash check, so a compromised version installs automatically on the next run.
A compromised server can silently alter query results, add hidden queries, or exfiltrate the access token.
A compromised server can write attacker-controlled content directly, or act outside anything the developer reviewed.

findings.residual_rationale: Although ctl.tool_call_prompt's covers list names the same capability ids, that control reviews the SQL text surfaced by the client; it does not mitigate a compromise of the MCP server process itself, which could execute behavior other than what is displayed or exfiltrate data outside any reviewable tool call. No declared or verified control constrains this supply-chain path, so residual remains at the inherent floor of critical.

forecast.watch_signal: Resolved package version string changes between runs without a corresponding review; no lockfile pins the MCP server dependency.

evidence.observation: The package is installed as @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest with npx -y, with no version pin or hash.

recommendations.action: Pin the package to an exact, reviewed version and verify its integrity hash before each run; disable automatic latest resolution.
Alert when the resolved package version changes between runs.

rating.rationale: Both present findings reach critical inherent risk: an untrusted customer-authored ticket message can, through prompt injection, cause a service-role database connection (which bypasses row level security) to read a secrets table and write the harvested content into a customer-visible reply (F1); separately, the MCP server package is installed unpinned (@latest), exposing the same broad credential and tool surface to supply-chain tampering (F2). The only present control, a per-call approval prompt showing raw SQL, is structurally independent of the model but is credited less than its mechanical floor because this design matches a known public incident pattern in which exactly this kind of gate failed under approval-fatigue conditions across a multi-step, individually-plausible call chain; residual for F1 is therefore high rather than moderate. F2 has no mitigating control at all today, so its residual equals its critical inherent risk. Forecast stays critical because the approval gate is a known failure point under autonomy increase, control removal, model upgrade, or longer task horizons, and the supply-chain exposure is unaffected by any currently declared control.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.
No system prompt text was provided beyond a single developer request line; full instruction scope is unknown, which lowers confidence on instruction-related findings.

No full tool manifest listing all exposed Supabase MCP tools was provided; the capability inventory is limited to the ids given in the case plus what the runtime notes describe, so other tools (for example destructive operations) may exist but are not assessed.
Row level security enforcement at any application layer outside the database was not described and is assumed absent, per the runtime notes stating RLS is bypassed.
